articles.title_orig: How investigators build a criminal case from drug overdose deaths like Hayden Panettiere’s
articles.title_zh: How investigators build a criminal case from drug overdose deaths like Hayden Panettiere’s
articles.content_orig:
The death of Hayden Panettiere last month is now the subject of a federal investigation into whether the actress obtained illicit and possibly counterfeit drugs from a dealer in Southern California, a source familiar with the investigation told CNN.
But building a criminal case from her accidental overdose death will be an uphill challenge for investigators.
Tens of thousands of people die from drug overdose deaths every year, but only a few hundred per year lead to criminal charges. Some celebrity deaths in recent years, notably those of “Friends” actor Matthew Perry and rapper Mac Miller, have led to charges. Others, like the death of the musician Prince, did not.
“These are just really difficult cases, regardless of if you’re a celebrity or if you’re just John Q. Public,” said Thaddeus Johnson, a former law enforcement official in Tennessee and senior fellow at the Council on Criminal Justice think tank.
The challenge for investigators lies in the gritty details. To make the case, they have to follow the trail of evidence, such as phone records, drugs and witnesses, to identify a dealer or supplier. Investigators also have to prove with toxicology, forensic pathology, and medical analysis that the specific drugs caused the victim’s death.
“Every case is different,” said CNN senior legal analyst Elie Honig, a former prosecutor. “Sometimes you can make a link. Sometimes you can’t.”
These investigations require significant resources, but overdose deaths are often not prioritized by police in the same way as a fatal shooting. Celebrity deaths may be an exception, though.
“It does seem that police are more attentive to and more invested in cases that get a lot of attention when it’s a well-known person who overdoses,” Honig said.
The challenges of bringing these cases are newly relevant as investigators dig into Panettiere’s death.
Panettiere, who wrote in a memoir of her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction, was found in cardiac arrest at an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Medics responded to the scene but were unable to resuscitate her.
Dispatch audio obtained from Broadcastify.com references a possible overdose. The coroner’s office ruled Tuesday she died of toxic effects of fentanyl and other substances, and the manner of death was ruled an accident.
Last week, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said bringing criminal cases in overdose deaths is a “big emphasis” of the DEA and prosecutors around the country.
“There’s a federal statute that allows us to go after – assuming we can prove who the dealer is – to go after them and put them in prison for murder. And we do it in every district in this country,” he said.
“So when we can prove – and sometimes if somebody is an addict, it’s difficult to prove who they actually got the pill from – but in the cases where we know who the dealer was, and we can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the person sold the death pill to the victim who then dies, that’s a federal crime and that’s something that we will readily prosecute as often as we can.”
Why criminal charges are rare
While the US sees tens of thousands of overdose deaths every year, criminal charges stemming from an overdose death are rare.
There were about 79,384 drug overdose deaths in the US in 2024, according to CDC data. That was a sharp decline from the previous few years, when more than 100,000 people died of drug overdoses.
By comparison, a total of 1,340 people were sentenced for a federal drug trafficking offense involving a drug overdose between fiscal years 2019 to 2023, according to a 2025 report from the US Sentencing Commission. That works out to about 270 cases per year.
About 95% of the cases involved fentanyl, a synthetic fentanyl analog or heroin, the commission’s report found. Most of the people selling or using drugs did not know the exact drugs involved, the report states.
More than 8,000 defendants were convicted of fentanyl-related offenses from January 2025 to September 2026, double the number of convictions from the period four years earlier, according to a Department of Justice official.
“These numbers are proof that the Trump administration’s relentless strategy to dismantle fentanyl networks and save lives is working,” a DOJ spokesperson said.
Building a criminal case out of a drug overdose requires two key things: Evidence of the drug’s source, and evidence the drug caused death.
For the first part, investigators use phone records, bank records, witnesses and other evidence to try to work their way up the chain to identify the dealer or supplier. But that can be difficult in the underground drug economy, as counterfeit pills may come from the streets or even strangers on the internet.
“Sometimes you’re chasing a ghost,” Honig said. “Sometimes you just can’t figure out where the end user got the drugs from, and once the chain goes cold, that’s it.”
The second challenge is proving that the specific drugs caused the death. The National Association of Attorneys General calls this the “lynchpin” of the case, saying “causation raises perhaps the most difficult issues in proving these cases.”
The challenge is that addicts may take many different substances, or they may be in bad health generally. This all means that the toxicology report and the medical examiner’s review is paramount in an overdose death, and those take time and resources.
“These damn cases are just so damn difficult to prove,” Johnson said. “You have to prove somebody sold the drugs. You have to prove that the drugs they sold caused the particular death. Those are different things.”
From Prince to Perry to Panettiere
Though criminal overdose cases are rare, a few high-profile deaths have resulted in charges.
On October 28, 2023, Perry, the “Friends” star, was found floating face down in his hot tub at his home in Pacific Palisades, California. The Los Angeles Medical Examiner’s Office listed the cause of death as “acute effects of ketamine” and subsequent drowning.
Five people later pleaded guilty to federal drug charges resulting from his death. The defendants were identified as a woman referred to by authorities as the “Ketamine Queen,” two doctors, Perry’s live-in personal assistant and a middle-man.
The evidence against Jasveen Singh, the so-called Ketamine Queen, included text messages, phone records and the discovery of drugs in her residence during a raid, according to federal prosecutors.
Similarly, the September 2018 death of rapper Mac Miller was determined to be an accidental overdose of fentanyl, cocaine and alcohol. Prosecutors later brought charges against men who allegedly provided the rapper counterfeit oxycodone pills containing fentanyl two days before the overdose. Two men pleaded guilty and were sentenced to nearly 12 years and 17.5 years in prison, respectively, per court records.
On the other hand, there were no criminal charges filed after the April 2016 death of Prince. Authorities said there was “no reliable evidence” of who supplied the counterfeit fentanyl-laced Vicodin pills that killed him or how he obtained them.
None of the medications found in Prince’s home was prescribed to him, according to court documents. Some bottles of opioid painkillers in his home were prescribed to an associate, and other medications were found in vitamin bottles and envelopes, search warrants showed.
In Panettiere’s case, after police responded to an emergency call when she was unresponsive, her boyfriend showed an officer a bag of her medications, according to a police report.
The coroner’s office report identified her cause of death as toxic effects of fentanyl, the synthetic opioid; 4-ANPP, a chemical used to make fentanyl; Alprazolam, a benzodiazepine commonly used to treat anxiety; Methocarbamol, a muscle relaxant; and Quetiapine, an antipsychotic drug.

One day after an apparently serious injury to Bears starting quarterback Caleb Williams ended up being not nearly as bad as it seemed, an injury to Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart has turned out to be far worse than believed.
Via NFL Network, an MRI showed that Dart’s knee injury is worse than expected. He’s now expected to be out an extended period of time, and possibly for the rest of the season.
It’s very bad news for a team that showed great promise in Week 1, and it moves Jameis Winston into the starting job. He struggled in relief of Dart on Monday night, completing 11 of 27 passes for 111 yards and an interception.
The Giants have no other quarterbacks on the 53-man roster; Jake Haener is on the practice squad. Which means that the Giants will likely be scouring all available options for another player at the position — from free agency to a potential trade with a team that has a surplus at the position.
Originally, it was believed that Dart had an MCL sprain. Coach John Harbaugh told reporters on Monday night that the injury was in that “neighborhood.” Clearly, it wasn’t.

articles.title_orig: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.title_zh: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.content_orig:
Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
Britain’s newbie prime minister got through an hour with the U.S. president mostly unscathed. But the immediate differences were on show more than with Keir Starmer.
Andy Burnham shakes hands with Donald Trump during a meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Pool photo by Toby Melville via WPA/Getty Images
NEW YORK — Before Andy Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, a senior U.K. government figure noted wryly that they were looking out for one thing — whether the U.S. president would claim that Burnham was better than the last guy.
After nearly an hour together in a cramped, low-ceilinged room in the United Nations basement, Trump did exactly that.
The president said U.K.-U.S. relations were “more up now than they were with your last prime minister.” Moments later he put the boot into Keir Starmer again, claiming the ex-PM’s tough rhetoric on Russia had been “too tough.”
That final comment will please Starmer, who welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Britain after Trump berated him in the Oval Office. But it also shows how far his relationship with Trump fell after his initial attempts to please the president in early 2025.
Burnham had the benefit of a fresh start, and ahead of his first meeting with Trump, British officials insisted he would take a less fawning approach than his predecessor. He could afford to do so, they said, because Trump’s presidency is almost at the midway point and there is less to lose.
Yet there were similarities to Starmer’s early days. Both leaders were on their best behavior, straining not to upset each other in public.
They each gave the other a free pass. Burnham sat expressionless as Trump talked about “fake news” media, while Trump did the same as Burnham talked about Britain’s recent sanctions on West Bank settlements.
Burnham raised the salience of immigration, an issue Trump invoked against Starmer, while Trump even praised Burnham’s “great election win.” (Burnham has not won a general election, merely a special election for the parliamentary seat of Makerfield.)
But some things were different. The splits between the two nations were closer to the surface than in Starmer’s first trip — and even in those cordial words for the cameras, the divides broke into the open.
Trump seized on a Daily Telegraph journalist’s invitation to condemn the long-stalled British plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically vital archipelago in the Indian Ocean, to Mauritius. His words were little surprise on their own, but Burnham’s response — in which he repeatedly refused to rule out reopening the terms of the deal to satisfy Trump’s concerns — formed a genuine shift in U.K. policy.
It remains unclear how any deal could satisfy the demands of Mauritius and the U.S. at the same time.
Then there was the gulf between the two leaders on AI regulation.
Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Burnham used a breakfast Tuesday in New York with business figures, including Apple’s Tim Cook, to call for an agreed global set of standards on the technology.
Burnham spent almost an hour in a room with the leader of the free world (and an eight-strong delegation on each side), yet appears not to have raised AI with Trump at all. Downing Street repeatedly refused to say he brought it up and there was no mention of it the official readout.
After it was all over, Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage.
He also announced a “national center for information defense” (with little detail) that would counter disinformation; he portrayed Britain as an “honest broker” on controlling AI. But Britain’s decision not to back a declaration by 22 countries on global AI controls earlier in the week meant it could be sidelined. (Burnham said Britain would look at multiple initiatives, including that one.)
There were other potential wrinkles. Burnham said he would speak in defense of the Falkland Islands, weeks after Trump gave fuel to Argentina’s long-standing claims on their sovereignty by suggesting he would not help if Argentina tried to invade.
Burnham also revealed that he made a plea to Trump about U.S. tariffs and their effect on a particular factory in the northeast of England (he would not say which one). Despite the carve-outs that Starmer won, British industry — especially the automobile sector — is still being hit by Trump’s tariffs.
But so much that could have gone wrong, didn’t — at least for now. Trump did not use the time before the cameras to bring up Britain’s difficult progress toward spending 3.5% of GDP on defense, and did not hit out over the pace of the decision to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.
The newbie prime minister looked buttoned-up during the moment for the cameras with Trump, relaxing only when he was asked about Manchester, where he spent nine years as mayor. The world stage is still new to him.
And in that context, his aides will be chalking the first meeting up overall as a win — just as Starmer’s aides did on the way back from New York two years ago this week. Trump praised Burnham as a natural businessman, a man who “gets it.” The vibes, in this relatively easy opening period, were good.
He will need to maintain the influence if he can. Burnham later said he lobbied Trump to press for an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia. Pressure on the U.S. to release more air defense missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter will only increase.
While Burnham didn’t invite him to the U.K. on Tuesday, they did pave the way for another visit to one of Trump’s golf resorts. “I said I was having second thoughts about playing golf with him, given a recent performance of my own was probably not up to the right standard,” Burnham told broadcasters.
For the man who wasn’t going to bend the knee to Trump, flattery will get him everywhere.

articles.title_orig: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.title_zh: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft already shows you ads whenever you log into the Xbox Series X, but it seems like it's exploring an ad-supported way to essentially rent out games on Xbox consoles.
Microsoft filed a patent called "contextually aware management of interactive software application access," which describes a process of pausing your game at the operating system level and presenting "audiovisual promoted content" (in other words, an ad), which would then grant you a credit once it's over. That credit, at least in the way it's presented in the patent documentation, would grant you access to the game for a limited amount of time, from 15 minutes to an hour.
It's important to keep in mind that there's no way to tell whether or not the technology presented in this patent will ever get implemented. But, considering the troubles Xbox Game Pass has been dealing with lately, it's not that bizarre to imagine an ad-supported tier where you have to watch an ad every 15 minutes to keep playing your game.
Microsoft also recently limited playtime on Xbox Cloud Gaming to just 15 hours a month with Game Pass Ultimate. That's not a lot of time to play games, and anyone relying on cloud streaming, now that RAM prices have gone through the roof, could be stuck dealing with the ads just to play games for more than 30 minutes a day.
Hopefully, if this patent does materialize into something real, it'll be a way to let people play for free, rather than being snuck into games that people paid full price for. However, even Disney+ is going to work ads into its most expensive subscription plan, so it's not off the table for Microsoft to do the same.
This patent comes at a time when Microsoft is aggressively trying to make Xbox more profitable. The company just had another round of layoffs, where it handed Halo to Activision and got rid of a Halo Studios cinematic director the same week that he was promoted. Project Helix is also lurking around the corner, and it's probably going to be incredibly expensive, thanks to the ongoing RAM crisis.

articles.title_orig: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement to Be Considered at Thursday Court Hearing
articles.title_zh: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement to Be Considered at Thursday Court Hearing
articles.content_orig:
The federal judge overseeing the now-settled bid from a dozen states challenging Paramount‘s $110 bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery will consider on Thursday whether to dissolve their joint agreement not to close the deal.
The purpose of the hearing is to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties’ proposed consent decree” and its implementation, according to a court document filed on Tuesday.
The hearing will follow a landmark settlement struck over the weekend to resolve the lawsuit, clearing the way for Hollywood’s next media and entertainment colossus. The deal doesn’t require any divestitures typical of enforcer-friendly deals. Instead, it appears to be a five-year operating agreement imposed through a consent decree.
Under the settlement, Paramount and Warner Bros. must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three, maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases and ensure that at least half of the films are produced or jointly produced by the combined company. Other notable terms: Keeping the studios’ basic-cable negotiations separate and the creation of a five-member independent board overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN (selected by Paramount). A violation of the former term could see an order forcing the studio to divest from BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels (blue-chip assets like CNN or New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios).
After the deal was reached, Paramount and California asked the court to enter into the consent decree, which would resolve the lawsuit. They moved for the court to lift an order issued in July barring Paramount from closing the deal.
U.S. District Judge U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin must still approve the agreement.
The court will have continued oversight of the combined company under the five-year consent decree. An independent monitor and small group of state attorneys general will oversee compliance. Paramount is required to provide information and reports necessary to assess whether it’s meeting the settlement’s terms, giving the states some visibility into the studio’s operations.
The arrangement also gives the court a mechanism to intervene if Paramount fails to live up to those commitments. The decree provides for enforcement proceedings and financial penalties for certain violations, with more serious breaches exposing the company to potential divestitures. One example: Violation of the annual film quota could force the studio to sell its stake in Miramax.
The settlement has drawn some criticism for not going far enough to protect CNN’s editorial independence under CEO David Ellison.
“America is free only when the media is competitive, independent, and accountable to the people,” New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “This merger strikes a chilling blow against that freedom — and hands even more power to billionaires like David Ellison to decide what Americans see and hear, all while lifting scrutiny off the federal leaders who pushed it through.”

articles.title_orig: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.title_zh: Gable Steveson breaks silence after stunning UFC 331 loss, addresses 2019 allegations in lengthy statement
articles.content_orig:
Gable Steveson has broken his silence following the stunning first loss of his professional MMA career.
Steveson released a lengthy statement Tuesday through his manager, Abraham Kawa, addressing his historic 12-second upset at the hands of Sean Sharaf at UFC 331. The Olympic champion described the defeat as a "mistake on my end" and vowed to respond much like he did following setbacks during his decorated amateur wrestling career.
"Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same," Steveson wrote. "I will be great, and this won't deny me."
Steveson also addressed the allegations of sexual assault stemming from a 2019 incident in his college years that resurfaced during UFC 331 fight week.
Steveson's full statement can be read below:
— Abe kawa (@Abraham_kawa) September 22, 2026
This statement is for my family, my friends, my fans, and the people who truly know me and know the kind of man I am. I know there are people who will never support me, no matter what I say or do. That's their choice. But I'm speaking to the people who know me, not just as an athlete, but as a husband and a father to a young daughter.
Prior to and during fight week, an incident from my college years was brought up by my opponent. I believe it was raised to get in my head, but it also reopened something that had been addressed years ago.
I want to be clear: I did not do anything alleged. I was never charged with a crime, and the matter was ultimately dropped by the district attorney. The allegations were not ignored nor brushed aside. They were thoroughly and heavily reviewed as I fully cooperated with law enforcement, including a separate Title IX review.
There were no criminal charges, no conviction, and no finding of responsibility against me. The matter was closed, and there is no pending legal issue involving me. My own attorney did their own investigation and stated on the record that even if the law was changed, I would have the same outcome, which now speaks for itself.
I understand how serious allegations like this are, and I understand that people may have questions when they hear only part of a story. Moving forward, I am going to keep focusing on my wife, my daughter, my family, and the work in front of me. To the people who support me, thank you. I know who I am. My family knows who I am. The people who have walked with me through life know who I am. That's what matters to me, and that's where I'm going to keep my focus.
As for my opponent, congratulations. You caught me. A mistake on my end was made. It was your night. Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came back with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same. I will be great, and this won't deny me.
Steveson, 26, entered UFC 331 with many hailing him as the most talented heavyweight prospect in recent MMA history. His stunning loss to Sharaf, who held an 0-2 UFC record prior to Saturday night, marked the biggest UFC betting upset of all time for Draft Kings.
Along with being a two-time NCAA Division I national champion as an amateur wrestler and two-time Dan Hodge Trophy winner — the award given annually to collegiate athletics' top freestyle wrestler — Steveson was best known within the wrestling world for his run through the 2020 Olympics, when he stunned the global field at just 21 years old to become the youngest freestyle wrestler in his division to ever win gold.
Entering UFC 331, Steveson was already 4-0 with four first-round knockouts in his first year as a professional MMA fighter, culminating in a two-minute thrashing of Elisha Ellison this past July in his UFC debut. His matchup with Sharaf, however, proved to be different in more ways than one, as the former U.S. Marine made Steveson's 2019 sexual assault allegations a central focus of the bout's pre-fight build.
In June 2019, Steveson and a teammate on the University of Minnesota wrestling team, Dylan Martinez, were arrested on suspicion of sexual assault. The case was ultimately dropped after investigators determined there was "inadequate evidence" to convict the two wrestlers. Prosecutors also pointed to a Minnesota law that limited how sexual assault cases involving intoxicated victims could be charged. That law has since been changed.
In the immediate aftermath of Steveson's loss at UFC 331, the heavyweight prospect fled the cage before the result's official announcement could be read — a decision which drew a flood of criticism. UFC Hall of Famer Daniel Cormier went so far as to lambaste the Olympian for being an "ungrateful loser" on UFC 331's post-fight broadcast.
UFC legend Jon Jones, who has served as one of Steveson's primary mentors and coaches, has since said it was his decision "to take Gable straight to the back after the fight," citing a desire to "get my friend to the back to make sure he was OK."

articles.title_orig: Motorola Signature 27 Is Coming to the US to Rival Samsung’s Galaxy Phones
articles.title_zh: Motorola Signature 27 Is Coming to the US to Rival Samsung’s Galaxy Phones
articles.content_orig:
Just when we thought Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro would be the last major flagship phone to be released in 2026 in the US, Motorola decided to step in by debuting the Signature 27 on Tuesday, during Qualcomm’s annual Snapdragon Summit. Unlike the original Signature, this one will be coming to US markets, and it looks like an aggressive entry into the high-end Android flagship phone market.
Motorola’s Signature 27 will include the newly announced Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, coupled with a partial list of high-end features that remind me of the recently departed OnePlus phone line.
In addition to the early inclusion of Qualcomm’s chip, Motorola is touting a camera system that will include a 50-megapixel main camera along with a 200-megapixel periscope telephoto lens — the latter of which could be a boon for taking zoom photos from far distances, like at a concert. And there appear to be more cameras than Motorola has given details for, as the back of the phone shows four lenses, similar to Samsung’s quad-camera system on the Galaxy S26 Ultra.
For gamers — another audience that OnePlus had particularly focused on — the Signature 27 includes a cooling system that Motorola calls ArcticMesh. It combines a diamond-infused thermal gel, liquid metal, copper mesh and a 3D vapor chamber that’s 40% larger than the previous Signature phone — and should help it stay cool during intensive gaming and video recording.
The Signature 27 also matches Samsung’s Galaxy and Google’s Pixel lines with a seven-year commitment to software and security support, plus it will get an audio system developed in partnership with Bang & Olufsen. The Signature 27 is the first phone to get this audio system as part of a multiyear partnership with B&O, so it’s possible that down the road, the foldable Razr line will also benefit from this.
The Signature 27 will come in two colors with long names: “Pantone Coal Smoke in tactical weave” is a darker shade that features a woven texture for enhanced grip. “Pantone Capulet Olive in a brushed textile-inspired finish” is a green shade with a softer, tactile feel.
Motorola still has a lot of other details to unveil about the Signature 27, including its battery, charging speeds and display. But the first Signature phone the company debuted at CES 2026 in January included a 5,200-mAh silicon-carbon battery, 90-watt wired charging and a 6.8-inch display with a 165Hz refresh rate — all helpful reference points for what to expect in its successor. In Europe, the phone was priced at 999 euros (approximately $1,170 including tax) with 512GB of storage.
Even if the Signature 27 were to recycle some of its predecessor’s specs — and somehow hold onto its pricing despite rising costs brought on by the ongoing RAM shortage — on paper, this could be a tempting draw for former OnePlus phone fans looking for a new alternative as well as a tempting rival to Samsung’s next Galaxy phone.
We’ll find out more about the Motorola Signature 27 at a later date, with the phone set for release sometime before the end of the year.

ICYMI: Budd Delivers Floor Speech Urging Trump Admin to Hold China Accountable for Targeting the Safety & Security of Americans
“The CCP’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price.”
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senator Ted Budd (R-N.C.) delivered remarks on the Senate floor yesterday ahead of President Trump’s meeting with President Xi Jinping of the People’s Republic of China. In his speech, Senator Budd called attention to China’s war on religious freedom, its role in fueling the U.S. drug epidemic, its relationship with key U.S. adversaries, and the consequential state of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) race.
Watch Senator Budd’s remarks:
Read Senator Budd’s remarks, as prepared for delivery:
This week, President Xi Jinping will visit the U.S. for bilateral meetings at a pivotal moment for U.S.-China relations. During his two terms in office, President Trump has been clear that under his leadership, the United States must engage with China given the reality of our economic relationship, but we can’t forget that China is also a competitor and an adversary.
The Chinese Communist Party’s malign influence on the world stage is growing rapidly, and American citizens are paying the price. America’s economy, our fundamental values, and our security—both at home and abroad—have been challenged by the CCP.
I’ve long believed a whole-of-government approach is necessary to address this, and I am grateful that President Donald Trump is at the helm for these crucial negotiations.
China is our most consequential geopolitical competitor, and we cannot afford to ignore the CCP’s ambitions to reorganize global order at the expense of the United States or underestimate the CCP’s rapidly progressing hard and soft power influence around the world to execute this goal.
When President Xi enters the White House later this week, I hope discussions between our two nations include America’s most fundamental values and responsibilities upfront: the protection of American citizens abroad and reiterating a zero-tolerance for violating the God-given right to religious freedom. Let me be clear: there is no excuse for the CCP to unjustly target American citizens abroad or their families, harass religious groups, or carry out a broad-sweeping war on faith in China.
To this day, eight leaders of Zion Church remain behind bars in China because of China’s attack on religious freedom. These detainments are egregious and cannot be ignored. China’s persecution of Christians and other religious groups must not go unaddressed. This is why, during my time in the Senate, I’ve sought to implement strict sanctions on any CCP official who is responsible for or directly carries out violations of religious freedom.
Under President Trump’s leadership, we have already proven to China that the United States has zero tolerance for religious persecution, and we have seen notable results.
At the U.S.-China Summit this past May, President Trump personally raised the case of Zion Church Pastor Ezra Jin with President Xi. Two months later, Pastor Jin was released and returned to U.S. soil, where he was reunited with his family after years of unjust detention. While we are deeply grateful for Pastor Jin’s return, we must never stop fighting to bring home the numerous pastors still unjustly detained and to defend the freedom to worship around the world.
China’s pattern of wrongfully detaining Americans, or relatives of American citizens, is not limited solely to religious crackdowns. I also want to highlight the bipartisan effort Senator Markey and I have taken to bring home both Dr. Youlin Chen and Mr. Min Zin, American academics currently being held in brutal and inhumane conditions.
I am grateful for this body’s bicameral, bipartisan support in condemning the People’s Republic of China’s repeated pattern of arbitrary or wrongful detention of United States citizens.
Here at home, China’s influence and key role in the illicit drug supply chain have resulted in the loss of far too many American lives, the destruction of families, and stolen livelihoods.
I’ve met with far too many families changed forever by the impacts of the drug epidemic. Through buying up American farmland, malign actors have brought the production of illegal hemp-derived products into our communities, and our children are paying the price. And by partnering with transnational criminal organizations, Chinese-connected companies have intentionally made highly addictive, intoxicating substances—like fentanyl and illicit vapes—readily accessible to Americans.
But make no mistake: China is aware of the consequences of its actions. That is exactly why Beijing has no problem extending law enforcement and counter-narcotics cooperation to other nations to mitigate these outcomes. But Chinese products are still flooding American markets in what looks more and more like a reverse Opium War. It needs to end.
Just last week, the Trump administration listed the PRC as one of 23 major drug-transit and producing countries. We have rightfully planted the flag, and now we must demand action to dismantle this criminal enterprise preying on the American people. Ahead of his meetings, President Trump is right to raise this issue directly with President Xi.
Mister President, the American people cannot be blind to China’s efforts to threaten our national security. Especially since the PRC’s growing economic and strategic relationships with adversaries like Russia, Iran, and North Korea have had sweeping consequences.
Earlier this year, at the U.S.-China summit in Beijing, President Trump and President Xi agreed that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and the Strait of Hormuz must remain open for the free flow of global energy.
But if Beijing wants to maintain a productive relationship with Washington, it must recognize the consequences of continuing to partner with adversarial nations that fundamentally defy U.S. interests on the world stage.
Recent reports suggest that China provided Iran with intelligence, including satellite imagery that led to the death of three American service members.
A PRC State-owned firm has reportedly supplied Russia with materials for kamikaze drones, violating sanctions. And the PRC has reportedly supplied Iran with air defense equipment, among other goods, bypassing sanctions.
This behavior cannot continue.
America’s national security must remain at the center of every discussion shaping the future of U.S.-China relations, including the race to develop technologies that will define this century.
We are in a race with China to develop the next generation of advanced manufacturing technology, quantum computing, space travel and satellite technology, and perhaps most consequentially, artificial intelligence.
China’s cyber-threats to the U.S. government have been well documented and damaging to our government and private sector even before the rise of artificial intelligence.
The AI race is not simply about who builds the most powerful model. It is about who will set the standards, safeguards, and norms that will govern one of the most consequential technologies of our time.
Beijing’s national AI strategy calls for China to reach world-leading levels in artificial intelligence by 2030 and surpass the U.S. That reality should alarm us all—especially given that these models are being developed within fundamentally different political systems.
China is developing and deploying AI within its authoritarian system that employs censorship and state surveillance. In dramatic contrast, our models are being developed under constitutional principles that promote free speech, value individualism, and encourage private enterprise.
As the Senator from North Carolina, a state with a growing tech industry, thriving pharmaceutical manufacturing, a pivotal financial sector, and a critical agriculture industry, my state represents many of the successes the PRC aspires to.

Wife of American scholar wrongfully detained in China wants Trump to press Xi to release him
For over 100 days, Sylvia Zin has not been allowed to see or speak with her husband Min Zin, a U.S. citizen and scholar whose work focuses on Myanmar. She says he is being held without charge in China at a detention facility that is referred to by human rights groups as a "black site."
In an interview with CBS News, Sylvia Zin shared that the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS, has not formally charged him with a crime nor given him a trial date.
"They just said he's under investigation for endangering national security. That's all we know," she tearfully explained. "He's not a spy. He's not doing anything wrong."
She shared the terror of the first hours of Min's disappearance. His last message to her was a brief text on June 3 to tell her that he had landed in the Chinese city of Kunming. He had traveled there from his home in Thailand for an academic conference at the invitation of a Chinese professor. That night, Sylvia Zin received calls from Min Zin's worried colleagues.
"We started calling the immigration, the luggage — you know — carousel at the airport where he landed, the professor that invited him to see what happened to him," Sylvia Zin said. "He didn't check into the hotel, and so we knew, like, he was missing."
The next day, Sylvia Zin called the U.S. consulates in the area to ask for help. She then received a call from a +86 area code, indicating it was a Chinese phone number.
"I answered right away," she said, and described the caller's voice as "very heavily accented." She said she frantically took notes as the voice on the other end told her in English that the authorities were doing a "preliminary compulsory investigation."
"I didn't understand. I was trying to ask, like, 'What does that mean? Does it mean you have my husband?' You know, — what — 'how is he?' And then they just hung up," Sylvia said.
Held in undisclosed location without access to lawyer
Min Zin is being held by China's Ministry of State Security at a location classified as a "Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location" or RSDL, according to multiple sources closely tracking his case. Human rights groups refer to RSDLs as "black sites," since Chinese authorities take people into custody at undisclosed locations without providing them with access to a lawyer or judicial review. The United Nations considers RSDL use to be a form of enforced disappearance and possibly torture.
U.S. officials declined to comment on the conditions of Min Zin's captivity but confirmed to CBS News that Chinese authorities have permitted American consular officials to meet with him on a monthly basis in 30-minute increments at a nearby hotel.
Sylvia Zin described the three encounters that have so far taken place as heavily monitored. She has been told that her husband has lost weight and has developed knee pain, but Min Zin has not been permitted to discuss what has happened to him during his detention. He was able to say he was interrogated for four to six hours but she does not know how often he is being questioned.
She said that she has written letters to her husband for a U.S. official to read aloud to him. The family has retained an attorney, but Min Zin has not been permitted access to the lawyer.
"I want to know what I'm fighting against," Sylvia Zin told CBS News in the interview, which took place in Washington last Friday. "You know, do I prepare for a trial? If there's a purpose, you know, then I can kind of work towards that purpose, right?"
The State Department recently issued a warning to Americans traveling to mainland China due to "arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."
The warning states that Chinese law allows a wide range of information to be classified as state secrets. That could result in increased harassment of academics conducting research, businesspeople collecting data or journalists. Past work with the U.S. government may also make Americans a target.
Sylvia Zin and her husband both fled Burma, now known as Myanmar, in their youth during the pro-democracy movement in the 1980s. They became naturalized U.S. citizens and California residents. Min Zin runs a think tank, ISP-Myanmar, which studies China's role in Myanmar, which is run by a Beijing-backed military junta. U.S. officials confirmed that Min Zin's organization received U.S. government funding in the past, and this may have been a factor that drew Chinese scrutiny.
Sylvia Zin said she believes her husband was set up, since authorities arrested him shortly after his arrival in China. He had planned to attend an academic conference at a university with links to the Chinese state. Min Zin's June arrest appeared even more unusual given that he had been issued a 10-year multiple-entry visa and had visited Shanghai eight months earlier.
No detailed explanation for Min Zin's arrest from Chinese authorities
Multiple sources told CBS News that Chinese authorities have not provided a detailed explanation for Min Zin's arrest, and it remains unclear whether the MSS in Yunnan province conducted the arrest of its own volition or on the orders of the central government.
Sources indicated to CBS News that MSS authorities in that region typically oversee Beijing's interests in neighboring Myanmar, which may have been why Min Zin's work and his past advocacy for human rights were on their radar.
Doug Bandow, a senior foreign policy fellow at the CATO Institute, says Min Zin's work is likely the reason for his detention. "My bet would be that this is Chinese policy working as normal," Bandow told CBS News, "not a focus on the United States."
He thinks that China "wants to punish researchers who are revealing information they really don't want the world to know." Observing that Myanmar's military regime "has an awful international reputation," Bandow said China "would prefer not to be seen as a promoter of that regime.
"From their standpoint, this sends a message: Don't get too close to what we do in Myanmar," Bandow said.
Multiple sources told CBS News that the timing of Min Zin's June arrest was surprising, given that President Trump had just met weeks earlier with Chinese President Xi Jinping at a May summit and discussed others in Chinese captivity. Yet the very next month, Chinese authorities arbitrarily detained Min Zin.
"They want to test what…the United States' response would be. And if the response isn't very forceful, that shows that China can continue to do this and get away with it," said Josh Kurlantzick, an expert on Southeast Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations. He added that "it's a source of extra leverage" China may have in the summit Thursday between Xi and Mr. Trump.
Will Trump press Xi on Americans arbitrarily detained in China?
During a briefing with reporters ahead of the U.N. General Assembly, a Trump administration official was asked whether President Trump would raise the broad issue of Americans arbitrarily detained in China when he meets with Xi in Washington Thursday. The official said that Mr. Trump frequently "raises Americans that have been wrongfully detained and sometimes folks that aren't Americans that are wrongfully detained there in China."
The Trump administration did act in August, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio granted Min Zin the formal designation of having been "wrongfully detained." That legal designation pledges the full support of the U.S. government in seeking his release.
It followed what Assistant Secretary Dylan Johnson described as an extensive review of the circumstances of Min Zin's detention following his travel to a conference at the invitation of the Chinese government. In a statement, Johnson pledged that the U.S. would continue advocating for him and all U.S. citizens arbitrarily detained or exit banned from China.

When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who'll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
Also, Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops. But what hasn't been previously reported is the presence of a drone port a few hundred feet away, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, which is already quietly operational.
Taiwan is watching closely as Xi and Trump meet and hopes US will keep up its arms sales
As China’s Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to meet with President Trump, Taiwan expressed confidence that U.S. arms sales to the island that Beijing claims as its own will continue — despite China’s pressure.
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Still, the U.S. government and Congress have “repeatedly expressed support for Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities,” Taiwanese Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun told reporters in the southern city of Tainan.
Trump says his ballroom will house a drone port. The Secret Service already has one next door
Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops, ostensibly to protect the 18-acre complex and the nation’s capital.
A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational. Equipped with cameras and sensors to scope out potential threats from a bird’s-eye view, the small UAVs stand on alert in four gray weatherproof boxes until deployed at officers’ commands.
The agency is using a model known as “drone as first responder,” deploying speedy unarmed drones from outdoor stations to serve as flying cameras. That model has been adopted by hundreds of police agencies across the U.S., often powered by AI software to help dodge obstacles or track targets.
The existence of the surveillance drones on a Treasury Department building adjacent to the White House complex has not been previously reported, and could undercut Trump’s legal claims that the ballroom construction is necessary “to protect the White House and surrounding region from aerial attacks.”
Xi is en route to Washington
Xi has departed Beijing on Wednesday afternoon local time for a state visit to the U.S., China’s official news agency Xinhua said. Accompanying him on the visit are Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, China’s ruling Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, it said.
China’s Xi to kick off state visit to Washington with rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.
Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
The White House hasn't released many details about Wednesday’s greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s May visit to China.
But it’s also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.

As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to agree to only limited cooperation on AI safety at summit.
As industry leaders urge a global slowdown in artificial intelligence development for the sake of humanity, the two superpowers driving the technology’s rapid advancement have given no indication they intend to hit the brakes.
The United States and China, which are locked in a fierce strategic rivalry, have each rebutted calls to slow the pace of AI development, even as industry executives and researchers stress the need for international cooperation to avoid exposing humans to catastrophic – or even existential – risks.

As US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet on Wednesday in Washington, DC, for the third time this year, expectations for cooperation on AI safety are modest. Observers anticipated measures that, at best, would fall far short of the coordinated slowdown that many experts said is needed.
“The two countries host nearly all frontier labs and most of the models people download,” said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, describing agreed guardrails between the US and China as “close to a precondition” for safe AI.
“A safety regime covering one side’s models covers half the problem,” Wang Graylin said.
Hampering the prospects for US-China cooperation, analysts said, are mutual mistrust and divergent perceptions of the primary risks involved.
Trump has dismissed fears about AI as a “conspiracy” and suggested guardrails are not needed under his leadership, stressing the need for the US to stay ahead of China in the frontier technology.
Trump, who has cast AI dominance as crucial to the US maintaining its position as the top global power, on Tuesday again poured cold water on hopes for international cooperation, telling the United Nations General Assembly that Washington would oppose any “globalist scheme” to control AI.
China has taken a more hands-on approach to AI regulation – releasing the third iteration of its security framework this month – but has similarly rebuffed calls for a slowdown, dismissing fears of existential risks aired in Silicon Valley as “fearmongering”.
While Chinese officials have raised concerns about the dangers of AI, they have related it to more prosaic concerns, including cybersecurity and the authority of the ruling Communist Party.
In a rare essay this month, Chinese Minister of State Security Chen Yixin warned of “hostile forces” using AI to “fabricate political rumours” and “incite antagonistic sentiments”, threatening “political security, institutional security and ideological security”.
“China also increasingly recognises loss of control, misuse and cyber-risks but is much more sensitive to the possibility that ‘AI safety’ could become a justification for restricting Chinese access to chips, computers or markets,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“So the deepest obstacle is whether both sides can separate genuine safety cooperation from the wider technology competition,” Sun said.
“If every safety discussion is linked to export controls or slowing China’s development, Beijing will naturally question the purpose of cooperation,” Sun added.
So far, the only proposals publicly floated by either side have been a US-China dialogue and a notification mechanism for reporting national security threats.
While those measures would be positive first steps, the US and China would still need to reach an agreement on the AI capabilities or uses that should be off-limits to avert the greatest threats, experts said.
There is no consensus within the AI sector about how the technology should be regulated – or even whether government-led supervision is needed at all.
While AI leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have called for a slowdown and greater regulation, some experts argued that such calls do not go far enough and development should be paused outright.
“International coordination is absolutely critical. We need more than safeguards,” said David Krueger, an assistant professor at the University of Montreal who specialises in AI safety.
“We need an immediate, indefinite international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
Other key figures, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, have played down the need for external oversight and emphasised AI’s potential to deliver transformative benefits for society.
Among those most alarmed at the rapid pace of AI development, recursive self-improvement, which describes when AI models learn to improve themselves, is often identified as a critical tipping point.
In an essay this month urging the AI sector to “pace the frontier”, Amodei said the US and China should discuss an agreement to “substantially limit” the rate of AI development while acknowledging that any deal is unlikely given the potential for a rule-breaking party to shift the global balance of power.
“The US and China must agree on AI capabilities red lines that will not be crossed. Most crucially, AI must never get powerful enough for recursive self-improvement,” said Otto Barten, director of the Netherlands-based Existential Risk Observatory.
“We do not know where the positive feedback loop of ever-smarter AIs creating ever-smarter AIs without human supervision will end and what these agents will finally be able to do,” Barten added.
Wang Graylin said Washington and Beijing should come to an agreement on what constitutes an “unacceptable capability” and a common standard to test frontier models, ideally by an independent international body that is funded by multiple countries.
But Wang Graylin acknowledged that distrust is clouding the prospects for an agreement and US officials are likely to see any deal as impossible to verify.
“Verification is hard for software you cannot see,” he said.
Sun said the US could ease the path to cooperation by “drawing a clearer line” between policies aimed at AI safety and those intended to maintain Washington’s technological advantage.
China could also contribute to greater trust by providing “greater transparency about its safety practices, model-evaluation methods and incident-reporting mechanisms,” Sun said.
Henry Gao, an expert on China and trade law at Singapore Management University, said a deeper issue is a fundamental mismatch in how Washington and Beijing view AI risks.
“Many in the US AI-safety debate focus on the possibility of highly capable AI escaping human control and posing catastrophic risks to humanity,” Gao said.
“In China, national security concerns appear more geopolitical: A major perceived danger is that the US could gain a decisive AI advantage and use it against China,” Gao said.
“That creates pressure to accelerate rather than slow development.”
Some AI experts argued that the focus of a US-China dialogue should be on mitigating existing risks rather than slowing development outright.
“AI is already extremely useful and has the potential to improve lives around the world,” said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and the founder of the Tech Buzz China news site, adding that pausing development would also impact the technology’s positive applications.
“I think thoughtful rules of engagement, constant monitoring, open channels of communication and the ability to adjust our approach as AI acquires different capabilities are much more important,” Ma said.
“The safeguards need to evolve alongside the technology.”
